title: Sort List
description: Brute force to optimized: an O(n^2) array-based sort versus merge sort adapted directly to a linked list's sequential access pattern.

blocks.text: Given the head of a linked list, return the list after sorting it in ascending order.

blocks.caption: Split at the middle using slow/fast pointers, recursively sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves

blocks.text: The linked list's nodes need to end up in ascending order by value, using the SAME nodes (typically), just re-linked into the correct order.

blocks.title: Analogy: Merge Sort on a Line of People, Not a Shuffled Deck
blocks.text: Since a linked list can only be walked forward (no direct "jump to the middle" like an array's index access), sorting it efficiently means adapting merge sort: repeatedly split the line of people in half (by walking two pointers, one twice as fast as the other, to find the midpoint), sort each half independently, then merge the two now-sorted halves back together by always taking whichever front-of-line person has the smaller value.

blocks.caption: The classic merge sort recursion tree: keep splitting in half until single nodes remain, then merge back up level by level

blocks.text: Before reaching for an O(n^2) approach (simple but slow), recognize that merge sort is the natural fit here, since it never needs random access, only splitting and sequential merging, both of which work fine on a linked list.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Sorting algorithms that rely on random access (like quicksort's partitioning around an arbitrary pivot index, or heapsort's array-index-based heap) are awkward on a linked list, since jumping to an arbitrary position requires walking from the head each time.

Observation 2: Merge sort only ever needs to (a) find a list's midpoint and (b) merge two ALREADY-sorted lists, both of which are naturally sequential operations, perfectly suited to a linked list's forward-only traversal.

Observation 3: Finding the midpoint reuses the exact slow/fast pointer technique from Middle of the Linked List, with one adjustment: the node just BEFORE the midpoint must be tracked, so its next pointer can be cut to null, splitting the list into two independent halves.

Observation 4: Merging two sorted linked lists reuses the exact technique from Merge Two Sorted Lists, using a dummy head and always attaching whichever list's front node currently has the smaller value.

Recognizing that BOTH of merge sort's core operations map directly onto previously-solved linked-list techniques (find-the-middle, merge-two-sorted-lists) is what makes this problem approachable despite sounding complex.
This is merge sort adapted to a linked list: recursively split at the midpoint (slow/fast pointers), then merge sorted halves back together (dummy head technique).
Extract every value into an array, and sort it using a simple O(n^2) algorithm like selection sort, ignoring the O(n log n) requirement, as a naive baseline for comparison.

items: Walk through the list, collecting every value into an array.
Repeatedly find the minimum of the remaining unsorted portion and swap it into place (selection sort), producing a fully sorted array.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Selection sort is used purely as an illustrative naive baseline; its O(n^2) time is exactly what the optimized solution must improve upon.

Working on a plain array sidesteps the linked-list-specific challenges (like finding a midpoint) entirely, which is precisely why it fails to meet the O(n log n) requirement expected of a proper solution.

blocks.text: Selection sort always produces a correctly sorted result, but its quadratic time complexity does not scale to the problem's constraint of up to 5*10^4 nodes.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2), due to the nested minimum-finding loop.
Space: O(n), for the intermediate array (plus O(1) if sorting were done truly in place on an array, though the underlying data structure here is a linked list).
Limitation: O(n^2) time is far too slow for the given constraints; merge sort achieves the required O(n log n) time and is naturally suited to a linked list's sequential-only access pattern.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force is a generic O(n^2) sort ignoring the linked list's structure. Instead, apply merge sort directly on the linked list: find the midpoint using slow/fast pointers (cutting the list into two independent halves), recursively sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves using the standard dummy-head merge technique.

Base case: an empty list or single node is already sorted, return it directly. Otherwise: find the midpoint (tracking the node just before it, so its next can be set to null), recursively sort both the left half (starting at head) and the right half (starting at mid), then merge the two sorted results.
Recursively split the list at its midpoint, sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The fully merged result is [1,2,3,4], matching the expected sorted output.

codes.python:
def get_mid(head):
    slow, fast, prev = head, head, None
    while fast and fast.next:
        prev = slow
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    prev.next = None                                                        # cut the list into two halves right here
    return slow

def merge(l1, l2):
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    tail = dummy
    while l1 and l2:
        if l1.val <= l2.val:
            tail.next, l1 = l1, l1.next
        else:
            tail.next, l2 = l2, l2.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = l1 if l1 else l2
    return dummy.next

def sort_list(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head
    mid = get_mid(head)                                                     # find the middle and split into two halves
    left = sort_list(head)                                                  # recursively sort the left half
    right = sort_list(mid)                                                  # recursively sort the right half
    return merge(left, right)                                               # merge the two sorted halves


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(4, ListNode(2, ListNode(1, ListNode(3))))
    result = sort_list(head)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), the standard merge sort recurrence: log n levels of splitting, each doing O(n) total merge work.
Space: O(log n) for the recursion call stack (the merging itself uses only O(1) extra pointers, reusing existing nodes).

Merge sort's correctness relies on a simple invariant: merging two ALREADY-sorted lists always produces a correctly sorted combined list, by repeatedly taking whichever front node is smaller. Since the recursion bottoms out at single nodes (trivially sorted), every merge step operates on genuinely sorted inputs, guaranteeing the final result is fully sorted.

items: getMid tracks "prev" (the node just before slow) specifically so its next pointer can be cut, physically separating the list into two halves.
merge uses a dummy head to avoid special-casing which list contributes the very first node of the merged result.
sortList's recursive calls operate on head (the left half, up to but not including mid) and mid (the right half), which only works correctly because getMid already cut the connection between them.

blocks.text: Sorting a linked list efficiently calls for merge sort specifically, since its two core operations (finding a midpoint, merging two sorted sequences) are both naturally sequential, unlike quicksort or heapsort which rely on random access.

items: Forgetting to cut the list into two truly independent halves (setting prev.next = null), which would cause infinite recursion or incorrect results.
Getting the slow/fast pointer midpoint-finding logic slightly wrong, producing an off-by-one split (which merge sort can still tolerate, but which should be understood precisely).
Reimplementing the merge step incorrectly, forgetting to attach the remaining (non-empty) list after one list is exhausted.

items: Explicitly naming the two reused sub-techniques (find-the-middle from Middle of the Linked List, and merge-two-sorted-lists from Merge Two Sorted Lists) demonstrates strong pattern recognition across the linked-list category.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Sort a LINKED LIST" (as opposed to an array) points strongly toward merge sort, since it avoids the random-access requirement that quicksort and heapsort rely on.

items: How would you achieve truly O(1) extra space (avoiding even the recursion stack)? An iterative, bottom-up merge sort (merging pairs of size 1, then 2, then 4, and so on) avoids recursion entirely.

Why is merge sort preferred over quicksort here? Quicksort's partitioning step relies on efficient random access to compare and swap arbitrary elements, which a linked list cannot provide efficiently.

How would you adapt this to sort a doubly linked list instead? The same splitting and merging logic applies, with the added step of correctly maintaining each node's "previous" pointer during merging.

Directly combines two previously-covered linked-list techniques in this category: the slow/fast pointer midpoint-finding from Middle of the Linked List, and the dummy-head merging from Merge Two Sorted Lists.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (linked-list merge sort): O(n log n) time, O(log n) space.

items: Pattern: Merge sort adapted to a singly linked list
Core Idea: Recursively split at the midpoint (slow/fast pointers), sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves using a dummy head
Time: O(n log n)
Space: O(log n) (recursion stack)
Most Important Observation: Merge sort's two core operations (find-the-middle, merge-two-sorted-lists) are both naturally sequential, making it the ideal sort for a linked list
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Split at the middle (slow/fast), sort each half recursively, merge with a dummy head
